summary: Lists a selection of characters, with mnemonics, and their presence in several coded character sets. It is informational and helps people compare character sets.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1345 gives every character a short name that does not depend on the character set it is stored in, such as a code for a letter with an accent. It then uses those names to list 145 character sets side by side and to describe a way of sending text that cannot be displayed on the receiving system without losing anything.

questions: how many character sets does rfc 1345 cover
subtitle: Short, unambiguous names for characters, and tables for the character sets of the world.

tldr.problem: As the Internet internationalised, text had to name characters such as accented letters and ideographs, but every character set used different numbers for them and the numbers changed between systems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1345 gives each character a short mnemonic written in characters that every character set shares, then uses those mnemonics to table 145 character sets and to define a way of sending any character without loss even when the receiving system cannot display it.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that specifies no standard. The character set names are registered with the IANA, and the memo says it may be updated periodically to reflect other coded character sets.

facts.label: Reference character set
facts.value: The 83 invariant graphical characters of ISO 646

today: RFC 1345 is an Informational RFC that specifies no standard, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. The memo says the character set names are registered with the IANA, that character sets not described in it should also be registered there, and that it may be updated periodically or supplemented by further specifications to reflect other coded character sets. It has no security considerations section.

sections.title: Why Character Mnemonics Were Needed
sections.content:
The memo starts from the internationalisation of the Internet, which made support for many coded character sets necessary. Its intention is to document precisely the mapping between characters and their coded representations in various coded character sets, and to give those character sets names so that they can be referenced unambiguously in Internet standards. The memo is careful about its own reach: it says nothing about the validity of using these specifications in any Internet standard, and tells the reader to consult each individual standard to see which character sets and names are allowed there.

The central idea is a mnemonic for every character that identifies it without reference to any coded character set and to the code that set gives it. The mnemonics are written in a minimal set of characters, the invariant 83 graphical characters of ISO 646. That set is described as a kind of greatest common subset found between the majority of coded character sets, including ASCII, the national variants of the ISO 646 7-bit character set and various EBCDICs. The numeric values of the coded representations of all of these characters are the same in every coded character set compatible with ISO standards, and all of them except two, the EXCLAMATION MARK and the QUOTATION MARK, have the same coded representation in all the variants of EBCDIC. This minimal set is called the reference character set.

The point of all this is practical. The mnemonics can be used in Internet standards for easy and unambiguous reference, and they can also serve as a fallback representation, so that a character which a system cannot display can still be written down and passed on.
sections.plainLanguage: A character like an accented letter has a different number in every character set, so naming it by number only works if everyone agrees on the set. This memo gives each character a short name built from characters that all the sets share, so the name travels with the text.

sections.title: How a Mnemonic Is Written
sections.content:
The mnemonics are taken from the ISO committee draft of the POSIX.2 standard, and they fall into two groups. One group uses two-character mnemonics and is aimed at alphabetic scripts such as Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Hebrew and Arabic, and at special characters. The other uses variable-length mnemonics and is aimed at non-alphabetic scripts such as Japanese and Chinese, and is also used for some accented letters and some special characters.

The two-character mnemonics draw on all the invariant graphic characters of ISO 646 except the ampersand: the punctuation marks, the digits, the Latin letters, both cases, and the underscore. The underscore is never used as the first character of a mnemonic. In variable-length mnemonics the underscore is also not used first, and if it appears within a name its presence is doubled.

Every mnemonic is given a long descriptive name, taken from the official ISO name of the character, with names of the same kind introduced by the memo for the few characters that ISO does not cover. These names consist only of the capital Latin letters of the invariant part of ISO 646, the digits, a hyphen and the space, and the digits appear only in the names of ideographic and Hangul characters and never first.

The mnemonic table itself has three fields: the mnemonic, which is mostly two characters; the ISO 2DIS 10646 code in hexadecimal; and the long descriptive name. The memo explains its caution about the second field: ISO 10646 was only at the DIS stage of development at the time of writing and was still much debated, but the long descriptive naming in the DIS was considered stable and the best official ISO reference to character names. The two-octet encoded value of ISO 2DIS 10646 is also given, but only as an identification of the character, because the coded representation may still change in the final international standard. Characters that are not in ISO 2DIS 10646 are allocated values in the private use zone and are given names and references to a character set where they are used.
sections.plainLanguage: Each character gets three things: a short code, a hexadecimal number used only to identify it, and a long official name such as LATIN CAPITAL LETTER A WITH RING ABOVE. The names are written using only characters that every character set shares, so they can be printed anywhere.

sections.title: Two-Character and Variable-Length Mnemonics
sections.content:
The two characters of a two-character mnemonic are chosen so that their appearance in the reference set resembles, as far as the available characters allow, the appearance of the character itself. The basic character set of ISO 646 is the reference set, and the characters in it are chosen to represent themselves. Control characters from ISO 646 use the two-character acronyms of ISO 2047 as mnemonics, and the other control characters of ISO 6429 have two-character mnemonics selected on the basis of the variable-length acronyms used in that standard.

For letters, including Greek, Cyrillic, Arabic and Hebrew, the base letter comes first and the second character stands for an accent or for a relation to a non-Latin script. Non-Latin letters are transliterated into Latin letters following transliteration standards as closely as possible. Latin letters such as ETH and THORN are transliterated in the same way, and the Danish, Norwegian and Swedish letter A WITH RING ABOVE becomes aa. The second character therefore has a fixed meaning in many cases: the exclamation mark is a grave accent, the apostrophe an acute accent, the greater-than sign a circumflex, the question mark a tilde, the hyphen-minus a macron, the left parenthesis a breve, the full stop a dot above, the colon a diaeresis, the comma a cedilla, the underscore an underline, the solidus a stroke, the quotation mark a double acute accent, the semicolon an ogonek and the less-than sign a caron. Other second characters point at a script rather than an accent: the equals sign means Cyrillic, the asterisk Greek, the percent sign a Greek or Cyrillic special, the four Bopomofo, the five Hiragana and the six Katakana, the zero a ring above, the two a hook and the nine a horn.

The variable-length mnemonics are meant chiefly for the ideographic characters in the large Asian character sets. To keep them short, which saves storage and makes them easier to type, the memo uses the row and column numbers that the Chinese standard GB 2312-1980, the Japanese standards JIS X0208 and JIS X0212 and the Korean standard KS C 5601 all use, each running from 1 to 94. Two positions for row and column plus a one-character set identifier is about as short as possible. The identifiers are c for GB 2312-1980, j for JIS X0208-1990, J for JIS X0212-1990 and k for KS C 5601-1987. The memo is honest that this scheme is not truly mnemonic, but says it provides short representations that are easy to connect to the character by way of the code table of an official standard, and that methods based on appearance or pronunciation are thought to be unfeasible.

The underscore is reserved as the delimiter for these longer mnemonics, at the front and the end, and the memo gives the example &_j3210_ &_j4436_&_j6530_. The ampersand is reserved as an intro character indicating that the following string is in the mnemonic character set.
sections.plainLanguage: A short code tries to look like the character it names, so a grave accent is written with the same characters that draw a grave accent. For Chinese, Japanese and Korean characters the code is instead a set letter plus a row and column number, which is short but says nothing about how the character looks or sounds.

sections.title: Naming and Tabulating the Character Sets
sections.content:
The character sets are named from the official ISO registration description in the ISO 2375 register kept by ECMA, or with a number such as the code page number, or with an indication of the language or country in which the set is used, using the country designators of ISO 3166. For the character sets in the ECMA register the ISO registration number is also given as ISO-IR-xxx. The memo notes that the registration number often does not cover every code of a set in use, for instance only the graphical characters when another registration covers the control characters, and that in the case of the 8-bit sets the registration covers only the upper graphical characters; here the registration number is taken to indicate the full coded character set, including the control characters and the lower half of the graphical characters, normally ISO 6429 and ASCII.

The memo quotes the ISO definition of a coded character set as a set of unambiguous rules establishing a character set and the one-to-one relationship between the characters and their coded representation, then sets out its own working definition: a set of rules that unambiguously and completely determines which sequence of characters, if any, is represented by each possible sequence of n-bit bytes for a certain value of n. One consequence is that a character set extended with others by the extension techniques of ISO 2022 is a character set in its own right. The memo uses the shorter word charset for this. It also notes the awkward question of whether two characters from different sets with the same descriptive name, or that look the same, or that share a historical origin, are really the same character; that problem was studied in detail in the work that produced ISO DIS 10646 and Unicode under the heading character unification, and as much as possible those results were used in constructing the code tables.

The code tables themselves are given in a simple format so that the text can be used directly as program input, and programs in C to handle them were freely available from the author. Keywords are marked with the ampersand as the first character so they can be told apart from ordinary data, and numbers may be decimal, hexadecimal with an x as the first character, or octal with an o as the first character.
sections.plainLanguage: Every character set gets a name, an official registration number where one exists, and a table in a plain format that a program can read. The keywords in that format start with an ampersand, so they never look like the characters they describe.

sections.title: Mnemonic Character Sets and Lossless Conversion
sections.content:
The mnemonic character sets are a family of character sets with one extra facility: inside the relevant parts of a message, encoded in an ordinary character set, the text may contain an intro character sequence followed by a string of characters that represent a character mnemonic. The intro character sequence may also be doubled, which indicates a single occurrence of that symbol in decoded form. Many characters in a mnemonic character set can be represented in two ways: normally the character itself is used, but the mnemonic allocated to the character may be used instead.

In this way every character with an assigned mnemonic can be represented without information loss in any character set that contains the invariant ISO 646 characters as a subset. The consequence is that, using a mnemonic character set, all of these characters can be generated uniformly on all keyboards and presented uniformly on all terminal equipment whenever the real character is not available. Data encoded in a mnemonic character set is intended to be read by the end user, possibly without further treatment; if the transport encoding and the presentation encoding for the user differ, the recommendation is to translate the data into a mnemonic representation in the presentation encoding.

A mnemonic character set is named mnemonic+charset+intro, where the charset is one of the names in the memo and is the encoding used for the transport; it cannot itself be a mnemonic character set. The intro is given as the decimal value of the intro characters in the transport character set, and there may be up to two of them; for a two-character sequence the value is the first character value multiplied by 256 to the power of the number of octets used in the character set, plus the second character value. The recommended value is 38, the ampersand in ASCII; other common values are 29, the Group Separator control character, and 8200, a space followed by a backspace. Only the ampersand may be chosen as intro from the invariant ISO 646 set, but any character outside that set may be used. Mnemonics longer than two characters are surrounded by the underline character, and the intro sequence is doubled to represent one occurrence of itself.

If the intro is specified as zero it is omitted from the transport, which gives more readable content but removes the possibility of reversibility and introduces information loss. With an intro of zero the underlines around longer mnemonics are removed as well, and the mnemonic character set mnemonic+ascii+0 is equivalent to the ordinary ascii set. The intro may also be given in a header named Mnemonic-Intro: with the value in decimal, which has meaning only if the character set can be deduced from other information and takes precedence over other information about the intro.

For compatibility, an application conforming to the memo that meets a mnemonic undefined by it shall leave the mnemonic as it is coded, which gives upward compatibility. When two parties agree to use different mnemonic character sets, a conversion can be made from the tables: characters present in both encodings are simply transformed, and characters that do not exist in the receiving character set are written as the intro character sequence of the receiving set followed by the character mnemonic, the characters forming the mnemonic being translated into the receiving code, which must contain them. A character that is undefined in the originating character set becomes the intro sequence, an underline, a question mark, a u for undefined, then the hexadecimal value of the character in lowercase, and a closing underline. Headers may need to change to match. The mnemonic /c has a special meaning: it says that a line is to be continued even when the next characters would otherwise specify a new line.
sections.plainLanguage: When a system cannot show a character, the text can still carry it: an ampersand introduces a short code instead, and the receiving system looks it up. Nothing is lost, and any two systems can convert between their character sets without losing anything on the way.

sections.title: What Is Covered, and What Is Not
sections.content:
The character sets covered include all parts of ISO 8859, ISO 6937-2 and all ISO 646 conforming character sets in the ISO character set registry managed by ECMA according to ISO 2375. Almost all the graphic character sets in that registry are covered; the ones left out are registry numbers 31, 38, 39, 53, 59, 68, 71, 72, 129 and 137. Many vendor defined character sets are covered as well, including PC codepages 4, 7 and 8, many EBCDIC character sets, and HP, DEC and Apple character sets. The East-Asian 16-bit character sets from the ECMA registry are also included. The memo's tables define 145 character sets in all, among them ANSI_X3.4-1968, the ISO 646 variants, BS_4730, the national variants from Denmark, Norway, Finland, Sweden, Italy, Portugal and Spain, the East Asian sets GB_2312-80, JIS_C6226, KS_C_5601-1987 and JIS_C6229, the ISO 8859 series from part 1 to part 9, and the EBCDIC sets for the United Kingdom and the United States.

The character set names are registered with the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority, and the memo says that character sets not described in it should also be registered with the IANA. It may be updated periodically, or further specifications may be published, to reflect other coded character sets, and comments, including comments about the accuracy of the tables, are to go to the author. The memo was produced with a grant from the Nordisk Industrifond, project number 91030, and the acknowledgements thank the people in the IETF 822ext working group and the many others who commented on the text and the tables.

The memo has no security considerations section.
sections.plainLanguage: The tables cover the international character sets, the East Asian ones, the national European variants and the common vendor sets, 145 in all. The names are registered centrally, so new sets can be added later, and the memo has nothing to say about security.

viz.caption: WHAT THE SECOND CHARACTER OF A MNEMONIC MEANS
THE KEYWORDS OF THE CODE TABLE FORMAT

cells: &charset
Gives the name of the character set. Required for every set.
&alias
Gives a possible alternate name for the character set. Optional.
&g0esc, &g1esc, &g2esc, &g3esc, &c0esc, &c1esc
Give the octet string that designates the set as the G0, G1, G2, G3, C0 or C1 set under ISO 2022.
&bits
Gives the number of bits used to represent the character set. Optional; 8 bits is the default.
&code
Gives the byte number allocated to the mnemonics that follow, which are listed in ascending order.
&code2
Gives the row and column in certain 16-bit character sets; 32 must be added to get the first and second byte.
&codex
Gives the set prefix string and the start and end row and column numbers.
&duplicate
Marks a position used for more than one character; takes the duplicated code and the new mnemonic.
&rem
Introduces a remark for a human reader.
&comb2
Specifies that a combination of two characters signifies a third.
